newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AUSTRALIAN BROADCASTING CORP MORNING UPDATE.
newsitem.headline: AUSTRALIAN BROADCASTING CORP MORNING UPDATE.

text.p: POLICE SCEPTICAL ABOUT BEAUMONT CLAIM
Senior police in Adelaide are sceptical about a claim by a Canberra woman that she is one of the missing Beaumont children.
Police say the matter could be settled quickly with scientific tests.
The woman's claim she is Jane Beaumont, the oldest of three children who disappeared from a suburban Adelaide beach in 1966, came to light when she approached a magazine with her story 18 months ago.
The magazine asked former detective Stan Swaine to investigate the claim.
He said there were enough similarities to warrant further investigation.
South Australian Assistant Police Commissioner Bob Lean is sceptical.
"We've got nothing concrete at this stage, she claims to be at various stages to be Jane Beaumont, but she's also using another name and has used other names, he said.
Assistant Commissioner Lean said DNA and fingerprint testing could decide the woman's claim, but she has disapppeared.
"She's taken her vehicle, and she's taken whatever, her dog and so forth, and so it indicates to us that possibly she's gone for not just overnight, she's gone for a while," he said.
FISCHER EXPECTS EXPORTER CONFIDENCE TO RISE
Acting Prime Minister Tim Fischer says he believes the confidence of Australian exporters will rise in coming months.
The Asia-Pacific Quarterly Export Indicator has revealed the confidence of exporters slumped in the past three months.
Speaking in Sydney last night, Mr Fischer said interest rate cuts and a smaller Budget deficit will help Australia's export industry.

"As we continue to build better market access to the world, as we improve efficiency and ultimately as we deliver genuine tax reform, GTR if you like, the full thrust of that agenda must be about easing the burden of indirect taxes on our exporters," he said.
Meanwhile, Mr Fischer said he is unable to give a date when Prime Minister John Howard will return to the political scene.
Mr Howard has been recuperating from pneumonia for the past two weeks.
Mr Fischer said the time for Mr Howard's return is between him and his doctors.
"He's in fine form, he's bouncing back, and it will be sooner rather than later," he said.
TALKS PUT A SINGLE RUGBY LEAGUE COMPETITION A STEP CLOSER
A single rugby league competition in 1998 appears closer with Super League and the Australian Rugby League describing a meeting between the sides yesterday as productive.

There have been a number of false dawns in the search for a compromise between the two rival competitions, but both sides believe a proposal put forward by ARL head Neil Whittaker may be a step forward.
The ARL's John Brady said both the ARL and Super League have agreed to refer a number of issues to their respective organisations.
"The feeling from Neil Whittaker after the meeting is that it was the most positive meeting to date," he said.
The proposal covers the the two major sticking points between the two parties; control of the finances and the operations of the game.
It does not however deal with the number of teams that would play in a combined competition.
THREDBO RESCUE OPERATION OVER
The Thredbo rescue operation is over with the final bodies removed from the landslide debris early this morning.
Rescue crews just managed to beat the bad weather which is now sweeping through the village.
The final three missing victims were found within a space of two hours in a spot emergency service workers had been concentrating on for the past 24 hours.
Their discovery brings to 18 the confirmed death toll from the landslide which caused the collapse of two ski lodges in the New South Wales resort town.
The lone survivor Stuart Diver is continuing his recovery in Canberra hospital.
The search effort ended just on a week since the tragedy.
Most of the victims bodies have now been identified by relatives, and the coronial inquest into the disaster can now begin.
Chief Superintendent, Eric Gollan, has praised the efforts of the hundreds of rescue workers who have contributed to the massive recovery operation.
But he said the job is far from over and work will continue on the site to ensure there are no more other victims beneath the rubble.

"Until we go through all of the site, until we sift through all of the debris, can we then say to the coroner that we are 100 per cent sure that we have completed our job in relation to human life," he said.
Meanwhile, it has been claimed that hundreds of the rescue workers on the scene at Thredbo will be severely out of pocket because of their efforts over the past week.
A church chaplain who has been with the rescuers throughout the ordeal says many of the volunteers are being docked by their employers.
Volunteer fire fighters, state emergency service workers and rescue squad members have been at the site since soon after the disaster hit.
Jindabyne Uniting Church minister Graham Abraham said many have told him of the loss it will mean to their pay packets.
"They don't get paid for a lot of their time, the professional crews they do, they get paid for being here," he said.

"But a lot of the volunteers that have come down, and we're talking about hundreds, most of them, by the time they get back and travel back to where they came from, will have lost close to a week's pay".
TAX CHANGES WILL HAVE LITTLE EFFECT ON PRICES SAYS ACCC
The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission believes tax changes announced this week, will have little if any impact on retail prices of petrol, alcohol and cigarettes.
The Commission will monitor any increase in prices, when the Commonwealth takes over collection of the taxes from the states.
Commission Chairman, Alan Fels, says his task is manageable.

"It involves just monitoring the prices of the people that actually pay the taxes, which are the breweries, the oil companies and the cigarette companies. That's only about a dozen companies," he said.
"Also, the Commission for years has been monitoring the effect of excise tax changes on those companies, so it's a fairly familiar task as well."
Meanwhile, there has been a blow to tobacco retailers' plans for a national class action, to recover millions of dollars in past franchise fees.
The Federal Treasurer, Peter Costello has said any money recovered through legal moves against the states will be taxed as a windfall profit, at 100 per cent.
QUEENSLAND GOVERNMENT'S PROBLEMS OVER SCRAPPED INQUIRY
The Queensland Government will face further legal action if it tries to complete a review of the corruption watchdog, the Criminal Justice Commission.
The Government has flagged the possibility of Attorney General Denver Beanland finishing off the review started by the aborted Connolly-Ryan Inquiry.

The Supreme Court ordered the multi-million inquiry be shut down immediately because inquiry head Peter Connolly was biased and his co-commissioner Dr Kevin Ryan lacked the power to complete the work.
Now the CJC has moved to recover its documents given to the inquiry and has asked for an undertaking that the material not be given to anyone, making it impossible to complete the review.
It says if the Attorney tries to subpoena the material it'll ask for another injunction.
But Premier Rob Borbidge has vowed to press ahead, saying the material will be used to formulate amendments to make the CJC more accountable.
HIGH JUMPER WINS AUSTRALIA'S SECOND MEDAL AT ATHENS
Timothy Forsythe has gained Australia's second medal at the World Athletics Championships in Athens.
The 1992 Olympic bronze medallist and current Commonwealth champion finished behind Cuban Javier Sotomayor who won the gold medal and Artur Partyka of Poland, the silver medallist.
Forsythe cleared 2.35 metres, just short of Sotomayor's 2.37.
It is Australia's second medal of the championships, following Cathy Freeman's gold in the women's 400 metres final.
